query: For rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability? State one controlled intervention that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that would support it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In rare-earth‐free high‐entropy alloys, a strong low‐field magnetocaloric response coexisting with rapid heat transfer, low hysteresis, and good mechanical stability is mediated by a controlled, magnetically‐driven spinodal decomposition that forms coherent nanoscale ferromagnetic domains (with dimensions well below the magnetic domain wall width). These nanodomains narrow the local distribution of exchange energies, enabling a superlinear increase of refrigerant capacity with applied field, while their coherent interfaces preserve high thermal conduction and mechanical robustness.
generation.material_initial_state: A fully disordered single‐phase rare‐earth‐free HEA (for example, a NiFeCoCr system with a low to moderate Pd content) produced by rapid quenching or as-rolled processing, characterized by a broad distribution of exchange interactions and a homogeneous (but not nanostructured) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored annealing protocol (e.g. a specific temperature and time schedule below the ordering temperature) to deliberately trigger magnetically‐driven spinodal decomposition, thereby generating coherent ferromagnetic nanodomains in the 10–50 nm range.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed on NiFeCoCr-based HEAs (with minor Pd additions up to ~11 at.%) under low applied magnetic fields (up to ~1 T) and temperature regimes around the magnetic phase transition (e.g. 100–200 K), where the nanostructure can both support magnetocaloric performance and allow rapid heat exchange.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of coherent nanoscale ferromagnetic domains (via spinodal decomposition) that narrow the distribution of exchange energies and produce clean interfaces with the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The coherent nanodomains yield a more uniform magnetic switching behavior, reducing hysteresis losses, and their small size (being below the domain wall width) minimizes pinning effects. Simultaneously, the defect-free, coherent interfaces facilitate rapid phonon and electron heat transfer, while preserving the mechanical integrity of the bulk. This dual role explains the simultaneous enhancement of magnetocaloric response and heat exchange without compromising mechanical stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to as-quenched or non-annealed baseline samples, the annealed samples with coherent nanodomains will exhibit a marked increase in refrigerant capacity (superlinear field dependence of the magnetic entropy change) at low applied fields, significantly reduced hysteresis in M(H) loops, improved measured rates of thermal exchange (e.g., via calorimetry during cycling), and retained or enhanced mechanical strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: Standard rapidly quenched or as-rolled HEA samples with a uniform, disordered microstructure lacking pronounced nanoscale phase separation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be operative in chemically complex, rare‐earth‐free HEAs where alloy additions (e.g., modest Pd content) and processing permit controlled spinodal decomposition; it may not hold for systems that undergo strong ordering transitions (such as Pt-induced L10 ordering) which dramatically increase coercivity or for alloys that develop incoherent or overly large phase segregations.
generation.uncertainty: While previous work (PMC4623812::web::012::magnetocaloric_effect) links improved refrigerant capacity to a narrowing of the exchange energy distribution via additive tailoring and annealing, and studies (PMC13030938::web::002::introduction) attribute low hysteresis to magnetically driven nanostructures, the combined effect on heat transfer and mechanical stability by coherent nanoscale domains is new. Uncertainties remain in optimally tuning the nanodomain size and coherence to balance these multifaceted properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NiFeCoCr-based HEA samples (with similar minor Pd content): one set processed by rapid quenching to retain a disordered microstructure (baseline) and a second set subjected to a controlled annealing protocol designed to promote coherent spinodal decomposition. Characterize the nanostructure via TEM to confirm the formation of ~10–50 nm coherent ferromagnetic domains. Then measure the magnetocaloric effect (magnetic entropy change and refrigerant capacity under low fields), hysteresis (M(H) loops), thermal exchange rates (using time-resolved calorimetry under cycling magnetic fields), and mechanical properties (tensile/compressive tests).
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for nanodomain size and coherence
Vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) for magnetization and hysteresis loops
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) or thermal cycling tests for heat exchange rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in low-field magnetocaloric performance (e.g., refrigerant capacity and entropy change), display similar or increased hysteresis, or show impaired thermal exchange rates and/or degraded mechanical properties compared to the baseline samples, then the proposed mechanism linking coherent nanodomain formation to the multifunctional performance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, we have achieved high magnetic anisotropy in rare‐earth‐free high entropy metallic thin films by sputtering and RTA. Robust magnetic order of both fcc FeCoNiMnCu and L10 (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt films has been demonstrated. The FeCoNiMnCu films exhibit a large coercivity increase after RTA, resulting from microstructural changes and strain‐induced anisotropy enhancement which strengthens domain wall pinning. Addition of Pt reduces the symmetry of the cubic fcc lattice to an intermetallic tetragonal L10 phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt. Although the Pt insertion lowers the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, the entropy is still high enough to stabilize an L10 single phase. This intermetallic phase is confirmed to host high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, likely attributed to the lower symmetry of the L10 structure and the strong spin‐orbit coupling provided by the Pt insertion. These findings demonstrate the promise of high‐entropy intermetallic design as a key avenue to search for new high‐entropy magnets beyond the equiatomic composition.
